x-m-el-ai-01.title: The average is 3.2 hours; how many hours is “typical” for our class?
x-m-el-ai-01.goal: In data with one extremely large value, judge using evidence that the mean and the median tell different things, then choose the value that shows what is “typical” and explain why.
x-m-el-ai-01.thinking.0: Evaluate with evidence whether a representative value describes the data well
x-m-el-ai-01.thinking.1: Explain the effect of an extreme value
x-m-el-ai-01.thinking.2: Look at the summarized value and the original data together
x-m-el-ai-01.prereq.0: Knowing what the mean, median, and mode each are (middle school level)
x-m-el-ai-01.prereq.1: Being able to list data in order of size and read it
x-m-el-ai-01.s.s1.prompt: When judging whether the presentation fits the data, what is the most convincing evidence?
x-m-el-ai-01.s.s1.hint.0: Count how many students played less than the mean of 3.2 hours and how many played more.
x-m-el-ai-01.s.s1.hint.1: Look at how the mean changes if you take out the value 13 hours and find it again.
x-m-el-ai-01.s.s1.o.a: The mean 3.2 is found by adding all the values and dividing, so it is the most trustworthy representative value
x-m-el-ai-01.s.s1.r.a: Using all the values can be a strength, but you did not consider that when one value is very large, it pulls the mean up.
x-m-el-ai-01.s.s1.o.b: 6 out of 10 students played 2 hours or less, so it doesn't fit “usually 3 hours”
x-m-el-ai-01.s.s1.r.b: This judgment didn't just look at the mean number; it counted where the students actually cluster.
x-m-el-ai-01.s.s1.o.c: 13 hours must be a mistake, so erase it and find the mean again
x-m-el-ai-01.s.s1.r.c: Erasing a value without a reason changes the data. First look at how much that value affects the result.
x-m-el-ai-01.s.s1.o.d: 3.2 is a decimal, so it's hard to say it in hours; the rounded 3 is right
x-m-el-ai-01.s.s1.r.d: You focused on tidying up how the number looks. You did not check whether 3 is close to the students' actual usage time.
x-m-el-ai-01.s.s1.explain: 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 2 is 6 students, more than half, and only 4 students played 3 hours or more: 3, 3, 3, 13. One student with 13 hours made the sum big and pulled the mean up to 3.2. The median (the middle of the 5th and 6th values) is 2 hours.
x-m-el-ai-01.s.s2.prompt: If you announced what is “typical” for this class in one sentence, which representative value (mean, median, or mode, any of them) would you use, and how would you handle the 13-hour value? Write your reasons.
x-m-el-ai-01.s.s2.hint.0: Count with numbers how many students each representative value describes.
x-m-el-ai-01.s.s2.hint.1: Check whether the value you chose is close to most of the students in this class.
x-m-el-ai-01.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you check with numbers from the data that the value you chose shows “most students”?
x-m-el-ai-01.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you decide how to handle the 13 hours without erasing it?
x-m-el-ai-01.s.s2.model.0: The median is 2 hours. The mean went up to 3.2 because of one student with 13 hours, so it fits the data better to say this class's typical is about the median, 2 hours, than the mean.
x-m-el-ai-01.s.s2.model.1: I'll show the mean of 3.2 hours and the median of 2 hours together. When there is a value that sticks out alone, like 13 hours, the mean alone makes it hard to know what is typical, and I'll explain that value separately instead of erasing it.

x-m-el-ai-02.title: Make data where the mean is 6 but the typical is 4
x-m-el-ai-02.goal: Make, yourself, a data set shaped so that the mean comes out greater than the median, and explain the reason using the numbers in your example.
x-m-el-ai-02.thinking.0: Make different data sets that meet the conditions
x-m-el-ai-02.thinking.1: Explain why the mean and the median differ
x-m-el-ai-02.thinking.2: Talk about cautions in choosing a representative value
x-m-el-ai-02.prereq.0: The meaning of the mean (sum ÷ number of values) and the median (the middle value when put in order of size)
x-m-el-ai-02.prereq.1: Calculating to match the sum of five integers
x-m-el-ai-02.s.s1.prompt: The mean of the five numbers came out greater than the median. What shape does the data generally have?
x-m-el-ai-02.s.s1.hint.0: Think about which of the mean and the median is affected more by a big value.
x-m-el-ai-02.s.s1.hint.1: Make a small example (1, 2, 3 and 1, 2, 30) and compare the two values.
x-m-el-ai-02.s.s1.o.a: The values are all similar and clustered in the middle
x-m-el-ai-02.s.s1.r.a: If the values are all similar, the mean and the median are almost the same. That isn't a reason the two values would come apart.
x-m-el-ai-02.s.s1.o.b: A few small values are much smaller than the rest
x-m-el-ai-02.s.s1.r.b: If small values are far away, the mean is pulled toward the small side. That is the opposite of the mean being larger now.
x-m-el-ai-02.s.s1.o.c: A few big values are much bigger than the rest
x-m-el-ai-02.s.s1.r.c: This is an idea that uses the fact that big values pull the mean up while the median depends only on the middle position.
x-m-el-ai-02.s.s1.o.d: The values are symmetric on the left and right of the middle
x-m-el-ai-02.s.s1.r.d: If it is symmetric, the mean and the median are equal. It can't explain why the mean is bigger.
x-m-el-ai-02.s.s1.explain: The mean reflects the size of every value, but the median is just the one value in the middle position. If there is a very large value, only the mean goes up a lot.
x-m-el-ai-02.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 different sets of five natural numbers that meet the conditions. Conditions: ① a ≤ b ≤ c ≤ d ≤ e ② the sum is 30 (mean 6) ③ the median c = 4 ④ only e is greater than the mean 6 (d is 6 or less).
x-m-el-ai-02.s.s2.hint.0: The sum is 30, so once you choose a, b, and d, e is decided automatically.
x-m-el-ai-02.s.s2.hint.1: Keep d from 4 to 6 and a and b at 4 or less, calculate e, and check whether e is greater than 6.
x-m-el-ai-02.s.s2.fail.c1: All five numbers must be natural numbers that are at least 1.
x-m-el-ai-02.s.s2.ok.c2: They are in order from smallest.
x-m-el-ai-02.s.s2.fail.c2: They are not in the order a ≤ b ≤ c ≤ d ≤ e.
x-m-el-ai-02.s.s2.fail.c3: The sum of the five numbers is not 30.
x-m-el-ai-02.s.s2.fail.c4: The middle value c is not 4.
x-m-el-ai-02.s.s2.ok.c5: Only e is greater than the mean 6.
x-m-el-ai-02.s.s2.fail.c5: d must be 6 or less and e must be greater than 6.
x-m-el-ai-02.s.s2.explain: With c = 4 and d ≤ 6, a+b+d is at most 4+4+6 = 14 no matter what, so e has to be at least 30−4−14 = 12. You kept the median at 4 and made only e large to bring the mean to 6.
x-m-el-ai-02.s.s2.because.prompt: Choose one of the examples you made, explain with its numbers why the mean became greater than the median, and write what to be careful about when describing what is “typical” for this kind of data.
x-m-el-ai-02.s.s2.because.hint.0: Look at the share the largest number e takes up in the sum.
x-m-el-ai-02.s.s2.because.hint.1: Think about what value a listener will picture if you only say the mean.
x-m-el-ai-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you explain why the mean and the median differ using the numbers of the example you chose?
x-m-el-ai-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you think about “how it would sound if you only said the mean”?
x-m-el-ai-02.s.s2.because.model.0: For example, with 2, 3, 4, 5, 16, one big value like 16 pulls the mean up to 6, so it is greater than the median 4. So if you use only the mean to say what is typical, it looks big.
x-m-el-ai-02.s.s2.because.model.1: In 1, 1, 4, 4, 20, the single 20 makes the sum big so the mean goes up, but the median is the middle value 4, so it stays the same. If you only say the mean, it sounds higher than most of the actual values.

x-m-el-ai-03.title: If the sum of errors is 0, is the model perfect?
x-m-el-ai-03.topic: Errors and the validity of predictions
x-m-el-ai-03.goal: Notice that simply adding errors can make the signs cancel out, and fix how errors should be combined when comparing models.
x-m-el-ai-03.material:
Models A and B made by a club predicted the test scores of 4 students. The error is calculated as (predicted score − actual score).
Model A's errors: +4, −4, +6, −6
Model B's errors: +1, +1, +1, +1
Below is how one student compared the two models.
x-m-el-ai-03.thinking.0: Find the leap in logic in the solution
x-m-el-ai-03.thinking.1: Compare the two models using the same standard
x-m-el-ai-03.prereq.0: The meaning of error = predicted value − actual value
x-m-el-ai-03.s.s1.prompt: Choose one line in the solution where the conclusion doesn't match the earlier calculation.
x-m-el-ai-03.s.s1.hint.0: For each of the students in A, check whether the prediction equals the actual score.
x-m-el-ai-03.s.s1.hint.1: Think about whether the sum being 0 and every error being 0 mean the same thing.
x-m-el-ai-03.s.s1.line.2: The sum of errors is 0, so Model A predicts everything accurately.
x-m-el-ai-03.s.s1.line.3: Model B's errors are four +1s and the sum is 4, so B is worse at predicting than A.
x-m-el-ai-03.s.s1.explain: Line 3: The errors have opposite signs like +4 and −4, so the sum just happened to be 0; in fact A was off by 4 to 6 points for every student. Line 4: B, with a sum of 4, was off by only 1 point each time, so its errors are actually smaller. Line 5 is a conclusion that relies on these two lines, so it falls apart with them.
x-m-el-ai-03.s.s2.prompt: Write which of A and B predicts more accurately, and how you should combine the errors to judge that.
x-m-el-ai-03.s.s2.hint.0: Think about whether you need the sign if you only look at “how far off” each student is.
x-m-el-ai-03.s.s2.hint.1: Calculate the size of how far off A and B are using the same method and compare.
x-m-el-ai-03.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you compare the “amount of error” of the two models with numbers?
x-m-el-ai-03.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you check that your method doesn't let errors with opposite signs cancel out?
x-m-el-ai-03.s.s2.model.0: B is more accurate. A's errors cancel out like +4 and −4 so the sum becomes 0, but if you take the average of the absolute values, A is 5 and B is 1.
x-m-el-ai-03.s.s2.model.1: If you square the errors and add them, A is 16+16+36+36=104 and B is 4, so choosing B is right. Errors with opposite signs cancel each other, so you shouldn't just add them.

x-m-el-ai-04.title: A line predicting scores from study time: how far can we trust it?
x-m-el-ai-04.topic: Errors and the validity of predictions
x-m-el-ai-04.goal: Tell apart predictions outside the range of the data (extrapolation) from predictions inside it, and revise how much you trust a prediction each time new information appears.
x-m-el-ai-04.material:
At one school, 5 students were surveyed about daily study time (1 to 5 hours) and mock exam score (out of 100).
(study time, score): (1 hour, 55), (2 hours, 65), (3 hours, 75), (4 hours, 85), (5 hours, 95)
The line score = 45 + 10 × study time passed through all five points.
x-m-el-ai-04.thinking.0: Evaluate the validity of predicted values
x-m-el-ai-04.thinking.1: Revise a judgment according to new data
x-m-el-ai-04.thinking.2: Tell apart prediction and individual differences
x-m-el-ai-04.prereq.0: Substituting values into a linear function
x-m-el-ai-04.prereq.1: Reading the range of the data and the maximum score as different things
x-m-el-ai-04.s.s1.prompt: The data are revealed one piece at a time. Each time, choose how to accept predictions made with this line.
x-m-el-ai-04.s.s1.hint.0: First compare whether the predicted value is possible in real life.
x-m-el-ai-04.s.s1.hint.1: Check whether the prediction is inside or outside “the range the data were collected in.”
x-m-el-ai-04.s.s1.st.0.info: If you put 6 hours into the line, you get 45 + 10 × 6 = 105 points.
x-m-el-ai-04.s.s1.st.0.ask: How will you take this prediction?
x-m-el-ai-04.s.s1.st.0.after: A score can't be over 100, and the line was made from 1 to 5 hours of data, so it isn't guaranteed outside the range (extrapolation).
x-m-el-ai-04.s.s1.st.0.o.a: The line passed through all five points, so trust 105 points as it is
x-m-el-ai-04.s.s1.st.0.r.a: Fitting the five points well does not mean it holds in ranges that weren't surveyed.
x-m-el-ai-04.s.s1.st.0.o.b: 6 hours will be the same as 5 hours (95 points), so predict 95 points
x-m-el-ai-04.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You changed the value without a reason. There is no evidence from the data for why it stops.
x-m-el-ai-04.s.s1.st.0.o.c: The full score is 100, so 105 can't happen, and outside the surveyed range (1 to 5 hours) the line may not fit
x-m-el-ai-04.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You compared the predicted value with real-world limits and kept the range of the data in mind.
x-m-el-ai-04.s.s1.st.0.o.d: 105 came out, so the line is wrong and this data can't be used
x-m-el-ai-04.s.s1.st.0.r.d: You threw away the whole line, which fits well inside the range. You didn't consider how far it can be used.
x-m-el-ai-04.s.s1.st.1.info: Two more students from another class were surveyed. The student who studied 7 hours scored 90 and the student who studied 8 hours scored 88. (The line predicts 115 and 125 points respectively.)
x-m-el-ai-04.s.s1.st.1.ask: Now, what is a valid way to use this line?
x-m-el-ai-04.s.s1.st.1.after: As study time gets longer, the rise in score may slow down. Trust the line only inside the surveyed range, and outside it build the model again with new data.
x-m-el-ai-04.s.s1.st.1.o.a: The 7- and 8-hour students are exceptions, so ignore them and use the line as it is
x-m-el-ai-04.s.s1.st.1.r.a: If you sweep away new data that doesn't fit as exceptions, you lose the chance to test the model.
x-m-el-ai-04.s.s1.st.1.o.b: Make the slope of the line steeper to fit the 7- and 8-hour scores
x-m-el-ai-04.s.s1.st.1.r.b: Making the slope steeper pushes the predictions even higher and farther from the new data.
x-m-el-ai-04.s.s1.st.1.o.c: The line is useless, so throw away all the data
x-m-el-ai-04.s.s1.st.1.r.c: The trend inside 1 to 5 hours is still useful.
x-m-el-ai-04.s.s1.st.1.o.d: Use it inside 1 to 5 hours, and outside that, put in new data and rebuild the model
x-m-el-ai-04.s.s1.st.1.r.d: This is a judgment that tells apart where the line fits and tries to fix the model with new data.
x-m-el-ai-04.s.s1.st.2.info: Among 20 students who studied 3.5 hours (inside the range), scores spread from 60 to 90 and the mean was about 79. The line's prediction is 45 + 35 = 80 points.
x-m-el-ai-04.s.s1.st.2.ask: How is it valid to explain this prediction to a student?
x-m-el-ai-04.s.s1.st.2.after: The line captured the average trend of students with the same study time (about 80 points) well, but one person's score has a large error, anywhere between 60 and 90.
x-m-el-ai-04.s.s1.st.2.o.a: The mean is 79, which differs from 80, so throw away the line
x-m-el-ai-04.s.s1.st.2.r.a: A difference of 1 point means the line captured the average trend well. You threw away the model over a small difference.
x-m-el-ai-04.s.s1.st.2.o.b: Say that the average trend is near 80 points, but an individual's score can differ from that by a lot
x-m-el-ai-04.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You told apart that the prediction is the average trend of a group and that an individual has error.
x-m-el-ai-04.s.s1.st.2.o.c: That student will get exactly 80 points
x-m-el-ai-04.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You did not take into account the fact that the scores of students who studied the same time spread from 60 to 90.
x-m-el-ai-04.s.s1.st.2.o.d: The scores are spread out, so the line's prediction has no meaning at all
x-m-el-ai-04.s.s1.st.2.r.d: Even with spread, the average trend still tells you something. If you declare it meaningless, you miss its usefulness.
x-m-el-ai-04.s.s1.reflect: How did your trust in the line change across the three steps? In what ways should you be careful about “a prediction outside the range” and “a prediction about an individual inside the range”?
x-m-el-ai-04.s.s2.prompt: To a friend who saw the ad line “Study 6 hours and you'll get 105 points,” write two conditions that should be added when stating the predicted value.
x-m-el-ai-04.s.s2.hint.0: Look again at what range the data used to build this line covered.
x-m-el-ai-04.s.s2.hint.1: Think about whether the scores of students who studied the same time were all the same.
x-m-el-ai-04.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Do the two conditions talk about different things?
x-m-el-ai-04.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Can you see how your conditions fix the ad line?
x-m-el-ai-04.s.s2.model.0: This line was built from 1 to 5 hours of data, so you shouldn't trust it as it is at 6 hours, which is outside the range. 105 points is even over the full score of 100. And a prediction is only an average trend, so scores can differ from person to person.
x-m-el-ai-04.s.s2.model.1: You need to say both that the prediction is outside the surveyed range of 1 to 5 hours, and that even with the same study time, scores have error.

x-m-el-ai-05.title: A spam filter with 99% accuracy: can we trust it?
x-m-el-ai-05.goal: Know that accuracy alone doesn't tell you whether a classification model is useful, judge what other information is needed, and build results yourself that have high accuracy but are useless.
x-m-el-ai-05.material: Of 1,000 emails, 10 are actually spam and the other 990 are normal emails. A company advertises a spam filter: “Our filter's accuracy is over 99%!” (Accuracy is the proportion of emails classified correctly.)
x-m-el-ai-05.thinking.0: Choose the information needed for a judgment
x-m-el-ai-05.thinking.1: Make cases where accuracy is high but the filter is useless
x-m-el-ai-05.thinking.2: Tell apart two kinds of classification errors
x-m-el-ai-05.prereq.0: Accuracy = number classified correctly ÷ total number (as a percentage)
x-m-el-ai-05.s.s1.prompt: If you could ask the developer only two things, what should you ask to judge whether this filter is worth using? Choose two.
x-m-el-ai-05.s.s1.hint.0: First sort out how many kinds of errors this filter can make.
x-m-el-ai-05.s.s1.hint.1: Think about how the accuracy number moves when there are as many as 990 normal emails.
x-m-el-ai-05.s.s1.o.a: Of the 10 actual spam emails, how many did the filter catch?
x-m-el-ai-05.s.s1.r.a: This is a question to check how many spam emails the filter misses. You noticed that accuracy hides this part.
x-m-el-ai-05.s.s1.o.b: How long has the company that made the filter been in the market?
x-m-el-ai-05.s.s1.r.b: A company's history doesn't tell you how well this filter classified these emails.
x-m-el-ai-05.s.s1.o.c: Of the normal emails, how many were classified as spam?
x-m-el-ai-05.s.s1.r.c: This is a question to check how often important normal emails go to the spam folder. You told the two kinds of errors apart.
x-m-el-ai-05.s.s1.o.d: What percent is the accuracy if calculated to two decimal places?
x-m-el-ai-05.s.s1.r.d: Even if you know the accuracy more precisely, it is still just one number. It can't tell you what errors are hidden.
x-m-el-ai-05.s.s1.explain: There are two kinds of classification errors: missing spam, and wrongly sending normal email to spam. Accuracy is a single number that merges the two, so when normal emails are far more numerous, you can get 99% even if you catch no spam at all. You need to know the number of each kind of error to judge whether it is worth using.
x-m-el-ai-05.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 different results for a filter that has accuracy of 97% or more but catches only 3 or fewer of the 10 actual spam emails. (tp is the number of spam caught, fp is the number of normal emails classified as spam. There are 990 normal emails, and the normal ones classified correctly are 990−fp.)
x-m-el-ai-05.s.s2.hint.0: Calculate how many of the 1,000 emails must be classified correctly for the accuracy to be 97% or more.
x-m-el-ai-05.s.s2.hint.1: Choose tp first, then find how large fp can get.
x-m-el-ai-05.s.s2.var.fp: Number of normal emails wrongly classified as spam
x-m-el-ai-05.s.s2.ok.c1: The numbers of emails are integers.
x-m-el-ai-05.s.s2.fail.c1: The numbers of emails must be integers.
x-m-el-ai-05.s.s2.fail.c2: The spam caught must be 0 to 10 and the normal emails wrongly classified must be 0 to 990.
x-m-el-ai-05.s.s2.fail.c3: The number classified correctly (tp+990−fp) is less than 970, so the accuracy is lower than 97%.
x-m-el-ai-05.s.s2.ok.c4: It caught 3 or fewer spam emails.
x-m-el-ai-05.s.s2.fail.c4: It caught more than 3 spam emails.
x-m-el-ai-05.s.s2.explain: If tp = 0 and fp = 0, even though no spam is caught, 990 emails are classified correctly, so the accuracy is 99%. Looking only at accuracy, a useless filter can get a high score.

x-m-el-ai-06.title: From what score do we call it “positive”?
x-m-el-ai-06.goal: Check with data that changing the classification criterion (threshold) makes missed cases and wrongly caught cases rise and fall in opposite directions, and choose a criterion that suits the situation.
x-m-el-ai-06.material:
A disease screening model gave 10 patients a “risk score” between 0 and 1. If the score is at or above the cutoff, it is classified as “positive (needs further testing).” The actual condition was confirmed later.
Risk score / actual condition:
0.95 disease, 0.85 disease, 0.75 healthy, 0.65 disease, 0.55 healthy, 0.45 disease, 0.35 healthy, 0.25 healthy, 0.15 healthy, 0.05 healthy
x-m-el-ai-06.thinking.0: Count errors for each criterion in a table
x-m-el-ai-06.thinking.1: Set a criterion according to the cost of the situation
x-m-el-ai-06.thinking.2: Explain what you accept when you change the criterion
x-m-el-ai-06.prereq.1: The two kinds of classification errors (missing, and wrongly catching) mean different things
x-m-el-ai-06.s.s1.prompt: The further test is simple and cheap, but if a disease is missed, treatment is delayed and it is dangerous. What is the best criterion for this situation?
x-m-el-ai-06.s.s1.hint.0: For each criterion, count how many of the 4 disease cases become positive.
x-m-el-ai-06.s.s1.hint.1: Compare which is the bigger problem in this situation: a healthy person becoming positive, or a disease being missed.
x-m-el-ai-06.s.s1.r.a: When the criterion is high, wrongly catching healthy people as positive decreases, but missing diseases increases. Compare which side is more dangerous in this situation.
x-m-el-ai-06.s.s1.r.b: This criterion makes it positive only when it is very certain. It is a choice made without counting how many diseases are missed.
x-m-el-ai-06.s.s1.r.c: It's in the middle, so it looks fair, but it didn't consider which error is worse in this situation.
x-m-el-ai-06.s.s1.r.d: This is a choice that puts first not missing the disease. In exchange, the number of healthy people classified as positive increases.
x-m-el-ai-06.s.s1.explain: With 0.4 or higher, all 4 disease cases become positive (0.95, 0.85, 0.65, 0.45), and 2 healthy people (0.75, 0.55) become positive too. At 0.5 or higher, you miss 1 disease case (0.45), at 0.8 or higher 2, and at 0.9 or higher 3. Missing is the more dangerous thing here, so 0.4 is right.
x-m-el-ai-06.s.s2.prompt: Now suppose a situation like “automatic cheating detection,” where a person who is wrongly accused suffers a big disadvantage. How would it be good to change the criterion? Write the direction and what you have to accept, using the numbers in the table above or a general explanation.
x-m-el-ai-06.s.s2.hint.0: Think about whether raising the criterion makes more or fewer people positive.
x-m-el-ai-06.s.s2.hint.1: Say what increases as the price of the one that decreased.
x-m-el-ai-06.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you say both that changing the criterion reduces one error and increases the other?
x-m-el-ai-06.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you check that the numbers or examples you gave match the table?
x-m-el-ai-06.s.s2.model.0: Raise the criterion. At 0.8 or higher, no healthy person becomes positive, but you'd miss 2 people who have the disease.
x-m-el-ai-06.s.s2.model.1: Raise the criterion and catch only when it is certain. In exchange, you have to accept that more people who really cheated are not caught.

x-m-el-ai-07.title: Planning learning experiments with a set budget and time
x-m-el-ai-07.goal: Under two limits (budget and time), make several plans that meet the goal, and judge that rounding the intersection point is not always a good plan.
x-m-el-ai-07.material:
An AI club runs two kinds of model-training experiments. Experiment X costs a budget of 3만 원 and 2 hours of computer time per run and earns a performance score of 4 points. Experiment Y costs a budget of 2만 원 and 3 hours per run and earns 3 points.
You can use a budget of at most 20만 원 and at most 18 hours of computer time. Experiments can only be run a whole number of times.
x-m-el-ai-07.thinking.0: Find solutions that obey several constraints at once
x-m-el-ai-07.thinking.1: Compare different plans that meet the conditions
x-m-el-ai-07.thinking.2: Verify that an estimated plan obeys the constraints
x-m-el-ai-07.prereq.0: Substituting values into linear inequalities to check true/false
x-m-el-ai-07.prereq.1: Reading and calculating expressions with two variables
x-m-el-ai-07.s.s1.prompt: Make 2 different plans where the total performance score is 25 points or more. (X is run x times, Y is run y times.)
x-m-el-ai-07.s.s1.hint.0: After choosing x, find the largest y that obeys both the budget and time expressions.
x-m-el-ai-07.s.s1.hint.1: Calculate both the budget 3x+2y and the time 2x+3y, and also check the score 4x+3y.
x-m-el-ai-07.s.s1.var.x: Number of times Experiment X is run
x-m-el-ai-07.s.s1.var.y: Number of times Experiment Y is run
x-m-el-ai-07.s.s1.ok.c1: The numbers of times are integers that are 0 or more.
x-m-el-ai-07.s.s1.fail.c1: The numbers of times must be integers that are 0 or more.
x-m-el-ai-07.s.s1.ok.c2: The budget (만 원) is 20 or less.
x-m-el-ai-07.s.s1.ok.c3: The computer time is 18 hours or less.
x-m-el-ai-07.s.s1.ok.c4: The performance score is 25 points or more.
x-m-el-ai-07.s.s1.fail.c4: The performance score 4x+3y is lower than 25 points.
x-m-el-ai-07.s.s1.explain: The plans that meet the conditions are (6, 1), (5, 2), (4, 3). (6, 1) has budget 20, time 15, score 27; (5, 2) has budget 19, time 16, score 26; (4, 3) has budget 18, time 17, score 25. (6, 0) has a score of 24, and (5, 3) has a budget of 21만 원, so it doesn't work.
x-m-el-ai-07.s.s2.prompt: A friend says, “The point where the budget and time are used up exactly at the same time is X 4.8 times and Y 2.8 times, so the rounded (X 5 times, Y 3 times) is the best plan within the limits.” How would you judge this claim?
x-m-el-ai-07.s.s2.hint.0: Put 5 and 3 into the budget expression and the time expression.
x-m-el-ai-07.s.s2.hint.1: Gather only the whole-number plans that obey the limits and compare their scores.
x-m-el-ai-07.s.s2.o.a: The intersection values are decimals, so there is no possible plan for this problem
x-m-el-ai-07.s.s2.r.a: Even with a decimal intersection, there are many whole-number plans. The plans you made in the earlier step are exactly such examples.
x-m-el-ai-07.s.s2.o.b: Directly substitute to check whether (5, 3) obeys the budget and time limits
x-m-el-ai-07.s.s2.r.b: This judgment checks whether the rounded values are also within the constraints. You told apart the first calculated value from the plans that are actually possible.
x-m-el-ai-07.s.s2.o.c: Decimal numbers of runs can't be used, so rounding is always the best within the limits
x-m-el-ai-07.s.s2.r.c: There is no guarantee that rounding obeys the limits. You generalized without substituting to check.
x-m-el-ai-07.s.s2.o.d: (5, 3) has the same score as (4, 3), so either one is fine
x-m-el-ai-07.s.s2.r.d: If you calculate the scores 4x+3y of the two plans, they are not the same. You didn't check the calculation.
x-m-el-ai-07.s.s2.explain: The budget of (5, 3) is 3×5+2×3 = 21 (만 원), which is over 20만 원. The time is 2×5+3×3 = 19 (hours), which is also over 18 hours. It breaks both limits. Among the possible plans, (6, 1) is the best, with a score of 27.

x-m-el-ai-08.title: Is packing the “best value first” always the best?
x-m-el-ai-08.goal: Find in a solution that the strategy of picking the best value-for-weight first is not always the best, and write a concrete counterexample and a revision of the claim.
x-m-el-ai-08.material: The weight a backpack can hold is at most 10kg. There are three items: A (6kg, value 30), B (5kg, value 24), and C (5kg, value 24), and each item can be packed only once. A student claimed, “If you pack the items with the greatest value per weight first, the sum of values is always the greatest,” and solved it as below.
x-m-el-ai-08.thinking.0: Find the overgeneralization error in a solution
x-m-el-ai-08.thinking.1: Give a counterexample with a concrete plan and numbers
x-m-el-ai-08.prereq.0: Finding the value per unit by division
x-m-el-ai-08.prereq.1: Listing the possible combinations within a limit
x-m-el-ai-08.s.s1.prompt: Choose one wrong line in the solution.
x-m-el-ai-08.s.s1.hint.0: Look for whether you can make a combination that doesn't pack A first, within the limit.
x-m-el-ai-08.s.s1.hint.1: List all possible combinations within the 10kg limit and compare their values.
x-m-el-ai-08.s.s1.line.0: Value per 1kg of weight: A is 30÷6=5, B is 24÷5=4.8, and C is 24÷5=4.8.
x-m-el-ai-08.s.s1.line.1: If you pack A, which has the greatest value per weight, first, 6kg is filled and the remaining limit is 10−6=4kg.
x-m-el-ai-08.s.s1.line.2: B and C are each 5kg, so they can't fit in the remaining 4kg.
x-m-el-ai-08.s.s1.line.3: Therefore the sum of values is at most 30, A alone.
x-m-el-ai-08.s.s1.line.4: So packing the items with the greatest value per weight first always gives the maximum value.
x-m-el-ai-08.s.s1.explain: Line 4: That is only the result when A is packed first; there is no basis that it is the only possible combination. Packing B and C together has a weight of 10kg, within the limit, and the value is 48, greater than 30. Line 5 doesn't hold because of this one counterexample.
x-m-el-ai-08.s.s2.prompt: Show with a concrete packing plan and its sum of values that this method is not always the best, and also write how to change this claim so that it becomes a true statement.
x-m-el-ai-08.s.s2.hint.0: Calculate the weight and value of one combination that doesn't pack A.
x-m-el-ai-08.s.s2.hint.1: Think about how to change the word “always” so it doesn't contradict the counterexample.
x-m-el-ai-08.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you recalculate to check that the weight and value sum of the counterexample are exact?
x-m-el-ai-08.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Does your revised claim avoid “always” or attach a condition?
x-m-el-ai-08.s.s2.model.0: Packing A alone gives 30, but packing B and C together gives weight 10kg and value 48, which is more. So the value-for-weight order is not always the best, and you have to compare all the combinations you can pack.
x-m-el-ai-08.s.s2.model.1: The method of packing the best value first has a counterexample. B+C is 48, but packing A first gives 30. So it should be changed to “sometimes the value-for-weight order may not be the best.”

x-m-el-ai-09.title: Finding students the pass-prediction model gets wrong
x-m-el-ai-09.topic: Finding cases where a model is wrong
x-m-el-ai-09.goal: Know that test data can miss a model's weakness, and make inputs that the model gets wrong yourself, then explain from their common point what information the model missed.
x-m-el-ai-09.material:
There is a model M that predicts whether students pass a school exam. Model M's rule is “If study time h is 4 hours or more, pass; otherwise, fail.”
In fact, the real pass standard of this exam is “h + s÷2 ≥ 6” (s is the sleep time the night before), but the person who built the model doesn't know this.
The 20 students who tested the model all slept 7 hours, and their study time was one of 1, 2, 4, or 5 hours. The model got all 20 students right, an accuracy of 100%.
x-m-el-ai-09.thinking.0: Make inputs the model gets wrong (counterexamples)
x-m-el-ai-09.thinking.1: Evaluate the limits of the test data
x-m-el-ai-09.thinking.2: Infer the cause from the common point
x-m-el-ai-09.prereq.1: Checking true/false of an expression with integer inputs
x-m-el-ai-09.s.s1.prompt: Seeing the 100% accuracy result, what students should you test next to best find where the model is wrong?
x-m-el-ai-09.s.s1.hint.0: Find what condition the test students all had in common.
x-m-el-ai-09.s.s1.hint.1: Think about whether the result would change if you changed information the model doesn't look at (sleep time).
x-m-el-ai-09.s.s1.o.a: Gather more students with the same condition (7 hours of sleep) as the existing test
x-m-el-ai-09.s.s1.r.a: Testing more in the same condition tends to show the same weakness. You didn't think about conditions that weren't in the test.
x-m-el-ai-09.s.s1.o.b: Gather 100 students with the longest study time
x-m-el-ai-09.s.s1.r.b: Extending only one end makes the tested conditions more biased. You can't make combinations that weren't in the test.
x-m-el-ai-09.s.s1.o.c: Gather students with sleep and study time combinations that weren't in the test
x-m-el-ai-09.s.s1.r.c: This idea uses the fact that the model may be weak in conditions the test didn't reach.
x-m-el-ai-09.s.s1.o.d: The accuracy is 100%, so no further testing is needed
x-m-el-ai-09.s.s1.r.d: You did not see that the conditions of the students used in the test were narrow. 100% means it is right only within those conditions.
x-m-el-ai-09.s.s1.explain: The test had the same 7 hours of sleep and had no boundary values like a study time of 3 hours. Cases where the model is wrong are usually outside the conditions used in the test. You have to change the conditions on purpose to reveal the weakness.
x-m-el-ai-09.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 different students (study time h, sleep time s) that model M gets wrong. The model's pass/fail prediction and the result by the real standard (h + s÷2 ≥ 6) must differ. h is an integer from 0 to 10, and s is an integer from 0 to 12.
x-m-el-ai-09.s.s2.hint.0: First, since the model looks only at h, think of a student whose h is 4 or more but whose sleep is very short.
x-m-el-ai-09.s.s2.hint.1: Conversely, also find a student whose h is less than 4 but whose sleep is long enough.
x-m-el-ai-09.s.s2.fail.c1: h must be an integer from 0 to 10 and s an integer from 0 to 12.
x-m-el-ai-09.s.s2.ok.c2: The model's prediction and the real result differ.
x-m-el-ai-09.s.s2.fail.c2: The model's prediction and the real result are the same, so the model gets it right.
x-m-el-ai-09.s.s2.explain: For (4, 3), the model predicts pass, but the real value is 4+1.5 = 5.5 < 6, so it is a fail. For (3, 6), the model predicts fail, but 3+3 = 6, so it is a pass. Errors occur in both directions.
x-m-el-ai-09.s.s2.because.prompt: Write what information the students you found have in common that the model missed, and how that makes it wrong.
x-m-el-ai-09.s.s2.because.hint.0: Put the h and s of the students you found side by side and look at which values the model looks at.
x-m-el-ai-09.s.s2.because.hint.1: Compare how the real results differ for two students with the same h but different s.
x-m-el-ai-09.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you mention that the examples you found are wrong in two directions?
x-m-el-ai-09.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you explain by connecting the information the model missed with the wrong results?
x-m-el-ai-09.s.s2.because.model.0: The model looks only at study time and doesn't consider sleep time. Even with 4 hours of study, if sleep is 3 hours, it's a fail, but the model says pass, and even with only 3 hours of study, if sleep is 6 hours, it's a pass, but the model says fail.
x-m-el-ai-09.s.s2.because.model.1: It's wrong because the information about sleep time is missing. It looks only at whether study time is 4 hours, so for students with very short or long sleep, the result comes out opposite.

x-m-el-ai-10.title: The moment a 98%-accuracy cat/dog classifier gets it wrong
x-m-el-ai-10.topic: Finding cases where a model is wrong
x-m-el-ai-10.goal: Re-examine, according to additional information, whether high accuracy shows a model's real ability, and design test data that finds in advance the cases where it is wrong.
x-m-el-ai-10.material: There is an AI model that looks at a photo and classifies it as “cat” or “dog.” On 500 test photos collected by the developer, the accuracy was 98%.
x-m-el-ai-10.thinking.1: Form a hypothesis about shortcuts (accidental clues)
x-m-el-ai-10.thinking.2: Revise a judgment according to additional information
x-m-el-ai-10.prereq.0: Classification models and the meaning of accuracy
x-m-el-ai-10.s.s1.prompt: Information is revealed one piece at a time. Each time, choose the best judgment about this model.
x-m-el-ai-10.s.s1.hint.0: Check what each piece of information tells you about “under what conditions the 98% came from.”
x-m-el-ai-10.s.s1.hint.1: Sort out what relationship animals and backgrounds had in the training photos.
x-m-el-ai-10.s.s1.st.0.info: We're going to put one new photo into this model.
x-m-el-ai-10.s.s1.st.0.ask: How well do you think this model will get a new photo right?
x-m-el-ai-10.s.s1.st.0.after: Here you still don't know what in the photo the model uses to get it right. Both the expectation that “it will do similarly well if the photos are collected the same way as the test” and the caution that “it could be lower if they're different” are reasonable.
x-m-el-ai-10.s.s1.st.0.o.a: If the photos are collected like the test photos, expect about 98% right
x-m-el-ai-10.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You read the accuracy as a result under the same conditions as the test.
x-m-el-ai-10.s.s1.st.0.o.b: It's 98%, so it gets any new photo 98% right
x-m-el-ai-10.s.s1.st.0.r.b: “Any photo” is a generalization added without evidence.
x-m-el-ai-10.s.s1.st.0.o.c: On photos in conditions different from the test photos, it could be lower
x-m-el-ai-10.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You were aware that the result could change on photos in conditions different from the test.
x-m-el-ai-10.s.s1.st.0.o.d: The accuracy number has no meaning, so you can't know anything
x-m-el-ai-10.s.s1.st.0.r.d: You threw away even the part that accuracy does tell you.
x-m-el-ai-10.s.s1.st.1.info: Most of the cat photos used for training were taken indoors, and most of the dog photos were taken on lawns or outdoors. The test photos were collected the same way.
x-m-el-ai-10.s.s1.st.1.ask: Can we say the 98% accuracy shows the “ability to tell cats and dogs apart”?
x-m-el-ai-10.s.s1.st.1.after: If there is a background rule of cat = indoors, dog = outdoors, high accuracy can come from the background alone, without looking at the animal. The test was collected the same way, so the weakness didn't show.
x-m-el-ai-10.s.s1.st.1.o.a: Yes, it shows it well enough. Because the test accuracy is high
x-m-el-ai-10.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You didn't examine whether the new information, that the test photos were collected the same way as the training, affects this conclusion.
x-m-el-ai-10.s.s1.st.1.o.b: Cats and dogs are animals that can't be told apart by photos in the first place
x-m-el-ai-10.s.s1.st.1.r.b: Before declaring they can't be told apart, you should first ask what the model looked at.
x-m-el-ai-10.s.s1.st.1.o.c: It might have gotten them right from the background only, so we can't be sure yet
x-m-el-ai-10.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You set up the shortcut (background) as a hypothesis for why accuracy is high. It's a judgment from which you can think of a way to check.
x-m-el-ai-10.s.s1.st.1.o.d: The background differs from photo to photo, so the model couldn't have learned it
x-m-el-ai-10.s.s1.st.1.r.d: You read it backwards: the background became a consistent, distinguishing clue.
x-m-el-ai-10.s.s1.st.2.info: When 20 photos of cats sitting on a lawn were tested, 14 were classified as “dog.” Of 20 photos of dogs sitting on an indoor sofa, 15 were classified as “cat.”
x-m-el-ai-10.s.s1.st.2.ask: What should you do to fix the model?
x-m-el-ai-10.s.s1.st.2.after: Accuracy dropped a lot on photos with mixed backgrounds (14 of 20 cats and 15 of 20 dogs were misclassified). Only when you find the cases the model gets wrong do you see the direction for fixing it.
x-m-el-ai-10.s.s1.st.2.o.a: Keep adjusting to raise the accuracy from 98% to 99% on the same test photos
x-m-el-ai-10.s.s1.st.2.r.a: Even if you raise the number on the same test, the background shortcut remains.
x-m-el-ai-10.s.s1.st.2.o.b: Include photos with mixed backgrounds, like dogs indoors and cats outdoors, in both training and testing
x-m-el-ai-10.s.s1.st.2.r.b: This is a judgment that you must change the data so backgrounds and animals are mixed, so the model looks at the animal itself.
x-m-el-ai-10.s.s1.st.2.o.c: Take the photos the model gets wrong because of the background out of the test to keep the accuracy
x-m-el-ai-10.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You removed the wrong cases and only protected the number. The weakness remains.
x-m-el-ai-10.s.s1.st.2.o.d: AI can't tell dogs and cats apart, so give up
x-m-el-ai-10.s.s1.st.2.r.d: You didn't use the clue that the cause is in the data.
x-m-el-ai-10.s.s1.reflect: What did you expect when you first saw 98%? How did your judgment change after you learned how the training photos were made up, and after you saw the wrong photos?
x-m-el-ai-10.s.s2.prompt: To a friend who wants to use this model trusting only the words “98% accuracy,” write concretely what photos they should test with to find in advance the cases where the model is wrong.
x-m-el-ai-10.s.s2.hint.0: Recall what condition always appeared together in the training photos.
x-m-el-ai-10.s.s2.hint.1: Imagine one photo where that condition is deliberately changed.
x-m-el-ai-10.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you say concretely how the photo you suggested differs from the training?
x-m-el-ai-10.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you connect what weakness would show up when tested with that photo?
x-m-el-ai-10.s.s2.model.0: You should test with photos where the background is the opposite of the training, like a cat photographed on a lawn and a dog photographed indoors.
x-m-el-ai-10.s.s2.model.1: You should test with photos collected evenly, with varied lighting, angles, and backgrounds. If the test is made the same way as the training photos, 98% can come out high.
